newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier says military reform will hurt.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier says military reform will hurt.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday military reform would be painful but drastic cuts were inevitable, Interfax news agency said.

Chernomyrdin told a meeting of Russia's top brass the long-promised reform should affect not only the armed forces proper but also border guards and troops controlled by other agencies, including the Interior and Emergencies ministries.
"We have to take decisive measures, including unpopular ones," Chernomyrdin said "This is needed for maintaining the country's defence potential."

Chernomyrdin made his remarks hours after Defence Minister Igor Rodionov fired a new shot in his battle for more funds for the cash-strapped army, saying that Russia faced a catastrophe unless it took extreme measures to reform the military.

"The armed forces today have come to the point where a further reduction in their combat readiness could lead to unforeseeable, tragic consequences," Interfax quoted Rodionov as telling another meeting of senior officers.
"If extreme measures are not taken to reform the army in the near future, the consequences for the state could be catastrophic."

Rodionov's comments, shown in television footage shot by NTV commercial television, stepped up his struggle to persuade the government to increase defence spending and pay soldiers who have not received their wages for months.
He has played down talk of a military rebellion but said repeatedly that the problems could soon get out of control unless defence spending is increased.

In a sign of top-level concern, President Boris Yeltsin discussed the state of the armed forces with Chernomyrdin in a telephone converstaion on Tuesday from the clinic where he is recovering after heart surgery.
A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin had specifically asked Chernomyrdin whether wages had been paid, as promised, to the armed forces.
Yeltsin promised during his re-election campaign last summer to scrap conscription and make the armed forces fully professional by 2000.
But top military officials and experts have made it clear that a desperate budget crisis made the deadline highly unlikely to be met.
Interfax quoted ground forces commander, Army General Vladimir Semyonov, as saying his forces would be reduced by reform to 10 or 12 fully equipped divisions.
According to research by the British-based International Institute for Strategic Studies, Russia currently has 47 mechanised infantry divisions and 17 tank divisions.
Semyonov urged that the loss in manpower be compensated by supplies of modern weapons and equipment.
Semyonov said there was in any case little chance the situation in the armed forces would improve before 2005-2010.
